title: Stop Trying to Hide Customers From Your Business
excerpt: AI is getting really good at handling customer calls, but here's the thing nobody wants to admit: deflection isn't the goal.

content.text: So here's something I've been seeing a lot lately, and it's kind of backwards: companies are bragging about how many customer calls their AI is handling without connecting to a human. And I get it — fewer humans on the phone means lower costs, right? But that's measuring the wrong thing entirely.

The real issue is that "call deflection" has become the success metric when it should actually be a warning sign. When you're celebrating how many customers never reach a person, you're accidentally celebrating how many customers you're *avoiding*. That's not a win. That's a ticking time bomb.
What Actually Happens With Deflection-Focused AI

Here's the pattern I'm seeing: A business sets up an AI system to handle customer calls. The AI gets better at keeping people in the automated menu. The company looks at the deflection numbers — "Hey, we're handling 70% of calls without human intervention!" — and they think they've won. But what they've actually done is train their AI to be really good at stopping frustrated people from reaching someone who could actually help.

The customers who get stuck in that AI loop? They're not happy. They're not saving you money by being efficient — they're getting mad, they're calling back, or they're just leaving to buy from someone else. You can't see that cost on a spreadsheet, but it's real.
The Better Way to Think About This

items: Let AI handle what it's actually good at: answering known questions, taking basic info, routing to the right department. That's legitimate.
Make it *easy* to reach a human if the AI can't help. This should be obvious, but it's not — most systems make you jump through hoops to escape.

Measure containment by *satisfaction*, not by avoidance. Did the customer's problem get solved? Great. Did they spend 15 minutes frustrated in a menu loop? Not great, even if technically you "handled" the call.
Use AI as a tool for your team, not a replacement for them. The best use case is AI gathering information before a customer talks to a human, not instead of a human.

content.text: The companies winning right now aren't the ones with the highest deflection rates — they're the ones where AI and humans work together so customers feel like their problem actually got solved.

content.label: Intecha's Take
content.text: If you're setting up AI for customer support, stop measuring deflection and start measuring whether your customers are actually happy. Train your AI to be helpful, not to be a gatekeeper. And for the love of everything, make it easy to get a human on the phone. You're not saving money by frustrating people — you're just losing them quietly.
